solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Effects of working at the farm

indicators.note: working suggests something being worked over and reshaped, so the letters of the next words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone describes what toiling on a farm does to a person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' looks like part of the farm scene, but it signals that AT THE FARM is to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the consequences or results that follow an event are its effects.

clue.text: The crime of war, so Napoleon said

indicators.note: of here means made out of, so the answer is taken from within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A quotation from Napoleon branding war a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'wAR SO Napoleon'; 'said' simply frames the surface as a quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: deliberately setting fire to property is a specific criminal offence.

clue.text: Accept bribes, perhaps, as a reporter should do!

definitions.meaning: bribes are often banknotes, so accepting them is taking notes in a money sense
a journalist writes down what is said at an interview or meeting

explanation.surface: A wry contrast between a corrupt official and a diligent journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: jotting down what is said is the reporter's job, while pocketing banknotes is the bribe-taker's.

clue.text: Pollyanna's visual aid?

parts.note: Pollyanna, the heroine of Eleanor Porter's novel, is relentlessly optimistic, so her spectacles would make everything look rosy

explanation.walkthrough: Pollyanna is a byword for incurable optimism; the cryptic idea is the pair of spectacles that colours every view cheerfully.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: an unduly optimistic outlook is described as seeing the world through rosy lenses.

clue.text: The Napoleon of crime was Sherlock's, he said

definitions.text: The Napoleon of crime was Sherlock's, he said

parts.words: The Napoleon of crime was Sherlock's, he said
parts.note: Holmes called Professor Moriarty the Napoleon of crime, and Moriarty was his greatest enemy

explanation.walkthrough: In Conan Doyle's stories Holmes describes Moriarty as 'the Napoleon of crime'; Moriarty is his chief adversary.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive: a principal enemy or greatest adversary, which Moriarty was to the detective.

clue.text: We join "stationary" flight, regardless

indicators.note: join here means the first word joins in the middle of the following flight, so it goes inside

parts.note: to hover is to fly while staying in one place
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invitation to join a flight that goes nowhere, whatever the circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'stationary' flag the paradox: a flight that stays put. 'join' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both words mean nevertheless or in spite of that, used to concede a point.

clue.text: Capone leaves in a panic, carrying a gun

indicators.note: leaves means goes away from, so the gangster's first name departs from the word for panicked

parts.note: to be alarmed is to be in a panic
Al Capone was the Chicago gangster

explanation.surface: The gangster Capone flees in a panic with a gun in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' removes AL from ALARMED.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: someone who is equipped with a weapon such as a pistol is armed.

clue.text: Broadcasts put on by the pretentious

definitions.meaning: to air a programme is to transmit it, so this is a verb meaning transmits
a snob puts on affected manners and graces

explanation.surface: Pretentious people show off what they transmit.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: affected manners are 'put on'; separately, a station transmits programmes on the radio waves.

clue.text: I go with the majority, being a bit wet

indicators.note: go with here means go along inside the group, so the single letter goes within the word for the majority

parts.note: most means the greater part, the majority
taken as written

explanation.surface: A conformist sides with the majority and ends up slightly damp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go with' puts I inside MOST.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: damp or slightly wet describes something with a little water in it.

clue.text: Players with the same score, presumably

definitions.text: Players with the same score, presumably

parts.words: Players with the same score, presumably
parts.note: the players are musicians performing a piece for two from one shared musical score, not sportsmen who are level

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tied game; the players are musicians sharing a score, performing a piece for two.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: performers of a piece for two voices or instruments read from the same music.

clue.text: Is in pursuit, we're told, of some Indians

indicators.note: we're told signals that what is heard, not what is written, gives the answer

parts.note: seeks means looks for, is in pursuit of

explanation.surface: Someone is chasing a group of Indians, according to reports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we're told' turns SEEKS into a word said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: followers of the faith founded in the Punjab are among India's peoples.

clue.text: Noel's reserve may indicate cold feet

parts.note: Noel Coward was the English playwright and wit
ice means cold reserve or aloofness of manner

explanation.surface: Noel's reticence might suggest nervousness.
explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward was a celebrated English playwright, so 'Noel's' is a name to complete, not a Christmas reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to get cold feet is to lose nerve, a form of lack of courage.

clue.text: The hourly grind, traditionally

parts.note: the conventional office working day runs from morning to late afternoon, the hours of the daily grind

explanation.walkthrough: 'hourly grind' plays on the daily grind, pointing to the standard office hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the phrase stands for an ordinary office job with conventional working hours.

clue.text: Instruction to restore original test

indicators.note: original means new or novel, so the letters of the following word take a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: An instruction to bring back the first version of a test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'original' rearranges TEST; the definition is the proofreader's mark meaning 'let it stand'.
explanation.definitionFit: Proofreading term: the Latin mark tells the printer to keep text that had been struck out.

clue.text: Very first twelve months, you might say

definitions.text: Very first twelve months, you might say

parts.words: Very first twelve months, you might say
parts.note: the opening year of any reckoning, such as the start of the calendar era, is spoken of with this phrase

explanation.walkthrough: 'you might say' signals a set phrase: the first year of an era, often used of something very long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the phrase means the opening year of an era, colloquially an extremely long time ago.

clue.text: Evil doctor and French NCO involved? Never!

parts.note: Dr No is the villain of the James Bond novel and film

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so these letters are mixed together

parts.note: et is French for and
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Bond villain teaming up with a French sergeant is flatly ruled out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges ET and NCO into TONCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an emphatic refusal meaning at no time whatever, on no occasion.

clue.text: Pain — one in lung area after injury

indicators.note: after injury means damaged and so knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A medical note: pain in a part of the lung following an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after injury' rearranges I plus LUNGAREA.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyponym: a sharp intermittent pain along a nerve is a type of pain.

clue.text: Weather's changeable, apart from capital — warms up again

indicators.note: changeable means liable to alter, so the letters are rearranged
apart from means except, and the capital is the first letter of the word, which goes

parts.note: read as the plural noun, weathers

explanation.surface: A forecast: the weather is variable except in the capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apart from capital' drops the W from WEATHERS, leaving EATHERS, which 'changeable' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: food that is heated a second time is warmed up again.

clue.text: Gas is unstable yet clean energy

indicators.note: unstable means not fixed in place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A warning that some supposedly clean fuel is volatile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is unstable' rearranges YETCLEAN into ACETYLEN; then add E.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the hydrocarbon used in welding torches is a flammable gas.

clue.text: Even bits of quilts, cut short, go to make overcoats

indicators.note: the even bits are the letters in the second, fourth and sixth positions of the word
cut means trimmed, so the final letter is lopped off

parts.note: terse means short or curt

explanation.surface: Pieces of quilting, trimmed, are made into coats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even bits of' takes ULS from qUiLtS; 'cut' trims TERSE to TERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a long loose belted coat of a style from Northern Ireland is a type of overcoat.

clue.text: Inclined to be shy about work

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word goes round the second

parts.note: to shy is to throw, to sling
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: Someone tends to be timid about their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shy' looks like timid but means throw, as in a coconut shy at a fair; 'about' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a surface that slants or is at an angle is inclined.

clue.text: Water features of Iceland old men reported

indicators.note: reported means spoken of, so the answer is a word heard the same as the other

parts.note: geezers is slang for old men

explanation.surface: A travel note about Iceland's sights and its elderly men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' turns GEEZERS into a word said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Iceland is famous for hot springs that shoot water into the air.

clue.text: See 3
In her heart Jacob's wife has to suffer

indicators.note: her heart is the middle of the wife's name, so the outer letters are dropped

parts.note: Rachel is Jacob's wife in Genesis

explanation.surface: Jacob's wife grieves inwardly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In her heart' strips the ends from RACHEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to feel a dull persistent pain is to suffer.

clue.text: Heads of hospitals, unlike matrons, almost never appear in person

indicators.note: heads are first letters, so the opening letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: Hospital chiefs, unlike matrons, hardly ever show up personally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads of' takes the initials of hospitals, unlike, matrons, almost, never.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a human being or individual is a person.

clue.text: Employment expert as a tormented man's psychiatrist?

parts.note: Job is the biblical figure tormented by God's trials
an analyst is a psychiatrist or psychoanalyst

explanation.surface: A careers adviser compared to a troubled man's therapist.
explanation.walkthrough: Job, in the Old Testament, suffered endless afflictions; here his name supplies the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a specialist who studies the duties and requirements of a particular post is an employment expert.

clue.text: Spruce up public transport

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: smart means spruce, neat and trim

explanation.surface: A call to smarten up the buses and trains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses SMART in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: streetcars on rails are a form of public transport.

clue.text: More than one statute book

definitions.meaning: laws passed by Parliament are statutes, here in the plural
the New Testament book of the Apostles follows the Gospels

explanation.surface: A statute book holding more than one law.
explanation.definitionFit: Double sense: laws passed by a legislature, and the fifth New Testament book.

clue.text: Golf eg, with some shots can win fortunes

parts.note: golf is an example of a game
chips are short lofted shots in golf

explanation.surface: Golf and a few good shots can make someone rich.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on chips used for stakes in a gambling game, which can win big money.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: gambling tokens staked at a casino table can bring big winnings.

clue.text: Nothing very much comes at the end

parts.note: O is the figure zero, nothing
mega is slang for very much, enormously

explanation.surface: Nothing much happens at the finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusion: the last letter of the Greek alphabet stands for the finish, as in alpha and the other.

clue.text: Virginal saint sang with ecstasy under torture

indicators.note: under torture means twisted, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A virgin saint sings in rapture while being tortured, as in a martyr legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under torture' rearranges SANG plus E.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the Roman virgin martyr celebrated on 21 January is a saint.

clue.text: Sort of great mess often found below stairs

indicators.note: sort means arrange, so the letters of the next words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sort of great clutter typically lurks in the space under the stairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges GREAT MESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: in British houses the utility meters are often in the cupboard under the stairs.
